title: Opsoclonus-myoclonus syndrome associated with multiple system atrophy
case_prompt:
A 48-year-old woman with a 7-year history of dopamine-nonresponsive parkinsonism and autonomic failure (diagnosed as multiple system atrophy–parkinsonian type) was admitted for 3 months of frequent episodes of dizziness (even when supine) and transient involuntary twitching of her upper limbs. Five years earlier she had developed postural syncope due to orthostatic hypotension and decreased sweating; over the past year she lost independent ambulation and developed dysphagia from pseudobulbar palsy.  

Medical history was notable only for treated hyperthyroidism. Family history was unremarkable.  

On admission, supine blood pressure was 136/74 mmHg, falling to 82/46 mmHg at 45° head-up tilt. Neurologic examination showed mild cognitive impairment, hypophonia, severe dysphagia, rigidity and bradykinesia in all limbs, hyperreflexia, positive pathological reflexes in the lower limbs, diffuse muscle atrophy, and autonomic features (anhydrosis, orthostatic hypotension, constipation, dysuria). She had recurrent, asynchronous, arrhythmic myoclonic movements of the upper limbs and abdomen at rest, which were also stimulus-sensitive. Very mild cerebellar ataxia was present; there was no palatal tremor.  

Ophthalmologic evaluation revealed involuntary eye movements consisting of repetitive, rapid, random, multidirectional conjugate saccades of irregular amplitude and frequency, present at rest and exacerbated by attempted gaze.  

Routine blood tests and cerebrospinal fluid analysis were normal. Serologic testing for HIV, herpes simplex virus, Epstein–Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, varicella-zoster virus, Japanese encephalitis A and B viruses, and JC virus was negative. Autoimmune panels—including antinuclear, anti–double-stranded DNA, antineutrophil cytoplasmic, antithyroid, and antiphospholipid antibodies—were negative. A paraneoplastic CSF panel (anti-Hu, anti-Ri, anti-Yo, anti-Ma/Ta, anti-VGKC, amphiphysin, anti-gliadin antibodies) was unrevealing.  

Electroencephalography during myoclonus showed only generalized slowing without epileptiform discharges; somatosensory evoked potentials did not demonstrate giant responses. Full-body CT showed mild right lower-lobe aspiration pneumonia but no primary or metastatic tumor. Brain MRI revealed linear T2/FLAIR hyperintensities in the putamina bilaterally and mild cerebellar and pontine atrophy. Tc-99m-ECD SPECT demonstrated hypoperfusion of the cerebral cortex, basal ganglia, and brainstem with only slight cerebellar hypoperfusion.
diagnostic_reasoning:
1. Paraneoplastic syndrome was considered given adult-onset OMS — “no elevation of tumor markers and was negative for paraneoplastic antibodies…CT of the thorax and breasts was also unremarkable…opsoclonus still persisted at two years after the onset of OMS…nothing suggestive of malignancies was found…paraneoplastic syndrome was considered to be excluded.”  
2. Parainfectious or direct CNS infection was considered — “other possible etiologies, such as parainfectious syndrome, direct infection of the brain…were excluded from the clinical course, antibody studies, normal CSF findings, and brain MRI findings.”  
3. Cerebrovascular disease was considered — “other possible etiologies…such as…cerebrovascular disease…were excluded from the clinical course, antibody studies, normal CSF findings, and brain MRI findings.”  
4. Autoimmune disease was considered — “other possible etiologies…such as…autoimmune disease were excluded from the clinical course, antibody studies, normal CSF findings, and brain MRI findings.”  
5. Primary neurodegenerative cause (MSA-P) was considered upon exclusion of other etiologies — “We therefore considered that this patient had OMS accompanied by advanced MSA.”
